We have mass spec: m/z 179.0946 (intensity 100) likely molecular ion [M+H]+? Usually mass spec gives m/z of molecular ion. The formula we derived from isomers list: C10H13NO2. Let's calculate exact mass: C10=120.000, H13=13.101, N=14.003, O2=31.989 => total 179.093. Indeed matches 179.0946. So molecular weight ~179.09, matches.

Proton NMR: signals: 2.58 (t, J=7.4, 2H), 2.84 (t, J=7.4, 2H), 3.81 (s, 3H), aromatic region: 7.17 (ddd, 2H), 7.93 (ddd, 2H). So aromatic AA'BB' pattern typical of para-disubstituted benzene (two sets of equivalent protons). Two aliphatic CH2-CH2 (two triplets) suggests ethyl chain attached to something. 3.81 singlet 3H suggests methoxy group (OCH3). So structure likely: para-methoxy phenyl attached to something with ethyl chain and carbonyl? Let's think.

We have C10H13NO2. Contains N and O2. Methoxy adds OCH3 (CH3O-). That's C1H3O1. Leaves C9H10NO? Wait total C10, so remaining C9? Actually methoxy uses 1 carbon, 3 H, 1 O. Remaining: C9H10NO? But we have O2 total, so one O left. N present. So remaining part: C9H10NO? But we need to account for aromatic ring (C6H4) plus substituents.

A para-disubstituted benzene: C6H4 plus two substituents. One substituent is methoxy (OCH3). The other substituent must contain N and carbonyl maybe? The aliphatic CH2-CH2 suggests an ethyl attached to carbonyl? Could be an amide: -CH2-CH2-CO-NH? But we have only one N and one O left (since carbonyl O). So maybe it's an ethyl amide attached to aromatic carbonyl? For example, para-methoxy phenyl acetamide? That would be OCH3 on para, and -COCH2CH3? Wait that would be ethyl ester? Let's examine.

If we have para-methoxy phenyl attached to carbonyl (C=O) which is attached to ethyl (CH2CH3). That would be para-methoxy phenyl acetate? Actually anisic acid ethyl ester: p-methoxybenzoic acid ethyl ester (ethyl p-methoxybenzoate). That has formula C10? Let's compute: p-methoxybenzoic acid (C8H8O3) plus ethyl adds C2H5 => C10H13O3? That's C10H13O3, no N. Not match.

What about p-methoxy phenyl acetamide? That is p-anisidine? Wait anisidine is p-methoxyaniline (C7H9NO). Not match.

Our formula includes N and O2. Could be a para-methoxy phenyl attached to a carbonyl amide: p-methoxybenzamide (C8H9NO2) plus maybe ethyl? Actually p-methoxybenzamide is C8H9NO2? Let's compute: C8H9NO2? Wait benzamide is C7H7NO, plus methoxy adds OCH3 (C1H3O) => C8H10NO2? Not match.

But we have ethyl chain (CH2-CH2) attached to something. Could be N-ethyl? N-ethyl amide? For example, p-methoxy phenyl acetamide with ethyl on nitrogen: N-ethyl p-methoxybenzamide? That would have N-ethyl (CH2CH3) attached to amide nitrogen. That would give CH2CH3 (2H triplet? Actually N-CH2CH3 would show quartet and triplet maybe). But we have two triplets each 2H, typical of -CH2-CH2- attached to hetero atoms on both ends (e.g., -O-CH2-CH2-N-). The chemical shift 2.58 and 2.84 both in aliphatic region near hetero atoms. Could be -CH2-CH2- attached to carbonyl (CH2 next to carbonyl ~2.3) and next to N ~2.6. So maybe it's an ethyl amide: -CO-CH2-CH2-NH-? But we have only one N.

Consider structure: p-methoxy phenyl attached to carbonyl (C=O) which is attached to CH2-CH2-NH2? That would be p-methoxy phenyl propionamide? Actually phenyl-CO-CH2-CH2-NH2 (phenylpropionamide). But we have para-methoxy substituent on phenyl, and the chain is attached to carbonyl carbon (i.e., amide). So structure: p-methoxy phenyl -C(=O)-CH2-CH2-NH2. That would have O (carbonyl) and N (amide). The CH2 next to carbonyl ~2.3, CH2 next to NH2 ~2.7. Both appear as triplets due to each other. Good.

Now count atoms: aromatic ring C6H4 (para substituted). Methoxy adds OCH3 (C1H3O). Carbonyl carbon adds C=O (C1 O1). Chain CH2-CH2 adds C2H4. Amide NH2 adds N1 H2. Total C: 6+1+1+2 =10. H: aromatic H4 + methoxy H3 + chain H4 + NH2 H2 =13. O: methoxy O1 + carbonyl O1 =2. N:1. So formula C10H13NO2 matches! Good.

Now check NMR: aromatic protons 4 total as AA'BB' pattern at 7.17 and 7.93 (two doublets? but ddd due to meta coupling). Good. Methoxy singlet 3.81 (OCH3). Aliphatic CH2-CH2 triplets 2.58 and 2.84 each 2H. That matches.

Thus SMILES: p-methoxy phenyl carbonyl ethyl amide? Actually the chain is CH2-CH2-NH2 attached to carbonyl. So structure: CO-CH2-CH2-NH2 attached to aromatic ring with methoxy para.

SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)CCN

But need to ensure para substitution: COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)CCN where OCH3 attached to aromatic carbon, carbonyl attached to same ring at para position? In SMILES, we can write: COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)CCN. This places methoxy at position 1, carbonyl at position 4? Actually the ring is c1ccc(cc1) with substituents at positions 1 and 4 if we place them accordingly. The SMILES above attaches CO (methoxy) to the first aromatic carbon, and C(=O)CCN to the same carbon? Wait need to specify para: COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)CCN means methoxy attached to aromatic carbon at position 1, and carbonyl attached to aromatic carbon at position 4 (since after the ring closure we have C(=O) attached to the aromatic carbon after the ring). The pattern c1ccc(cc1) indicates positions 1-6; the first 'c' after the ring start is position 1 (attached to CO). Then after three 'c's we have (cc1) which includes positions 4 and 5? Actually typical para substitution SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)CCN is correct for p-anisoyl ethyl amide? Let's verify: anisoyl ethyl amide would be p-methoxybenzoyl ethyl amide (C6H4-CO-CH2CH3 with N?). But we have amide with NH2 not ethyl. Wait our chain is -CH2-CH2-NH2, not -CH2CH3. So the SMILES is COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)CCN. That matches.

Check formula: Let's compute using tool.
